newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's MMBG seems dead as Telekom quits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's MMBG seems dead as Telekom quits.

text.p: Germany's ill-fated digital television consortium Multimedia Betriebs GmbH on Monday appeared close to collapse after its leading shareholder announced it would leave the group.
Deutsche Telekom AG, the telecommunications giant which holds 27 percent of MMBG, said it would inform other shareholders this week of its plans to withdraw from the group.
"We want to pull out," said Telekom spokesman Hans Ehnert, confirming a report in the Suedduetsche Zeitung newspaper. He would give no further details.

Telekom is MMBG's largest shareholder. Other investors include Bertelsmann, Compagnie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT), French pay TV group Canal Plus, TV network RTL and public broadcasters ARD and ZDF.
MMBG was set up to market a common digital decoder for its shareholders and avoid a battle over technology standards akin to the war between VHS and Betamax video recorders.

But this goal was undermined by Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, who declined to join the group, launched his own decoder and assembled a powerful arsenal of pay TV programming for his DF1 digital pay TV channel, which went live in July.

The takeover of the Dutch Nethold group by Canal Plus also changed the landscape. Canal Plus now controls Europe's two decoder systems -- the Seca decoder it created with Bertelsmann and Nethold's Igeto decoder, which is being used by Kirch.
The aquisition means MMBG has become irrelevant as a standard-setting group. Canal Plus now has the power to determine which decoder will be used in Europe.
As a result of this development, Telekom appears to be concerned that it could become dependent on Canal Plus and is moving to develop competing technology.
Some industry observers said Telekom's withdrawal from MMBG and the pursuit of its owns technology will further delay the development of digital television in Germany.
"You can forget about digital TV for the next two years," one industry source said on condition of anonymity.
MMBG shareholders would not comment on the group's future, but Telekom appeared to be just the first domino to fall.
"We are also considering our position," a Bertelsmann spokesman said.
The Sueddeutsche Zeitung said Telekom now plans to develop its own decoder. This would give it more control over how to integrate various digital programmes into its cable TV network.
Digital television was recently launched in Germany amid much hype and fanfare. But acceptance of the new medium appears to lag far behind expectations.
Bavaria media magnate Leo Kirch has spent billions over the past six months to lock up years of rights to digital pay TV programming from Hollywood movies to World Cup soccer.
BSkyB, the satellite pay TV network in which Rupert Murdoch's News Corp holds a big stake, dumped Bertelsmann and Canal Plus to take a stake in Kirch's DF1.

But DF1 seems set to fall short of its goal of signing up 200,000 subscribers by the end of the year. While Kirch gives no official figures on the numbers of DF1 subscribers, industry observers put the number at no more than 3,000.
One reason sales are so low is because DF1 programming is not compatible with Deutsche Telekom's cable TV network, which has some 16 million subscribers.
The industry has also failed to deliver the interactive programming it promised and German viewers are already satiated with nearly 30 programmes available on cable TV.
